To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the predictability of stock returns can be attributed to a set of lag macroeconomic variables, (2) the predictability based on macroeconomic variables is not limited to the US market but can also be found in the UK and Japan, and (3) momentum strategies are not profitable once the predictability of macroeconomic variables is accounted for.

1) the predictability of stock returns based on past stock returns (momentum) is due to the predictability of returns based on a set of lagging economic variables, 2) the predictability is not a result of the predictability of the economic variables by stock returns, and 3) the economic variables predict stock returns through time-varying risk premia.
momentum profits are not abnormal and are not a violation of market efficiency.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether momentum strategies are consistent with the notion of rational expectations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
momentum is an anomaly, but it is an anomaly which is fully explained by a time varying expected return model.
the momentum strategy is a rational strategy.
the momentum effect is not a real effect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we show that the time-series pattern in stock returns, which is the source of the momentum effect, is related to the time-series pattern of macroeconomic activity and that the momentum effect is not a source of abnormal profits.
the time-series patterns in asset prices can be explained by time-varying risk premia, which can be explained by changes in macroeconomic conditions and the business cycle.
the time-varying component of expected returns can explain momentum profits, and thus the momentum effect is consistent with rational market efficiency.
The main takeaway from our work is that
time-varying risk premia can account for momentum profits.
the time series patterns in stock returns can be explained by macroeconomic variables and that the momentum profits are due to the failure to adjust for time-vary-ing expected returns.
